analysis.one_liner: Makes executives and others repay pay and stock profits when the big banks they ran fail.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had 12 Senate cosponsors from both parties, never received a hearing or vote in the Senate Banking Committee and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: After the 2023 bank failures, this bill would have required the FDIC to take back up to three years of salary, bonuses, stock awards, and stock-trading profits from executives, directors, and shareholders who caused more than a minimal loss when a large bank fails. The recovered money would go into the government's deposit insurance fund rather than staying with the people who ran the bank into the ground. It also widened the FDIC's power to claw back pay from failed financial companies no matter how the FDIC was put in charge. The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary depositors and taxpayers benefit: when a large bank fails, the people who caused the loss would have to return pay and stock profits to the deposit insurance fund, reducing the cost that bank failures otherwise push onto the fund that protects everyone's accounts. It also raises the personal price executives pay for reckless management, which could discourage it in the first place.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Bank depositors and the insurance fund

how_it_helps.text: It requires the FDIC to claw back three years of salary, bonuses, performance pay, equity awards, and stock-trading profits from directors, officers, controlling stockholders, and others who caused more than a minimal loss at a large failed bank.
Any money recovered goes into the Deposit Insurance Fund, the fund that backs ordinary depositors' accounts, instead of being borne by the fund and ultimately by the banking system.
It expands the FDIC's existing clawback authority so it applies no matter which legal process put the FDIC in charge of a failed financial company.

analysis.who_pays: Executives, directors, controlling shareholders, and other participants in the affairs of large failed banks ($10 billion or more in assets), who would repay up to three years of compensation and stock profits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Executives and shareholders of failed banks

drawbacks.text: The clawback only takes effect after a large bank has already failed, so it recovers money after depositors, workers, and the insurance fund have absorbed the damage rather than preventing failure in the first place.

The bill's trigger — a party that 'caused more than a minimal financial loss' — leaves the FDIC significant discretion in deciding who is responsible and how much to claw back, which could make enforcement uneven.

It reaches beyond top executives to directors, shareholders, and others involved in a failed bank's affairs, so some people who had little control over risky decisions could still owe clawed-back compensation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is accountability: executives who run large banks into the ground would repay some of the pay they collected in the run-up, replenishing the insurance fund that backs everyone's deposits, and the threat of clawbacks could discourage excessive risk-taking. The main drawbacks: it applies only after a bank has already failed, so it compensates after the damage rather than preventing it; the "more than a minimal loss" trigger leaves substantial discretion to regulators, who could apply it weakly; and it reaches beyond executives to ordinary directors and shareholders who played little role in decisions, raising fairness questions. Still, the core mechanism is narrow and targeted at people who caused the failure.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with bipartisan sponsorship and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on June 1, 2023, in the wake of the spring 2023 bank failures.
Twelve senators cosponsored it, including five Republicans — Josh Hawley, Mike Braun, JD Vance, Katie Britt, and Kevin Cramer — alongside seven Democrats.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee, where it received no further action.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Executives and major shareholders of large banks are better off: no law now requires them to repay compensation when their banks fail, and the Deposit Insurance Fund absorbs those losses instead.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Executives and shareholders of large banks

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship crossed party lines — 7 Democrats and 5 Republicans cosponsored — but the bill never advanced beyond referral, so no roll-call votes exist to measure broader support.

industries.industry: Executives, directors, and major shareholders of large banks
industries.note: They would face personal repayment of up to three years of compensation whenever a bank with over $10 billion in assets fails and they contributed to the loss. Nothing like this currently applies automatically after a bank failure.
Clawback liability for failed-bank executives would raise the personal cost of reckless management and could constrain aggressive pay-for-risk practices at big banks.
Recovered compensation would flow directly into the fund that protects depositors, reducing the chance that losses from bank failures fall on the banking system and taxpayers.
